video_title: Christopher Merrill on Building $110B Harrison Street
gist: Christopher Merrill explains how Harrison Street grew from a $200M first fund into a ~$110B Colliers-backed platform by being a pure-play investor in need-based 'demographic' real estate (student, senior, medical office, storage) and now infrastructure and data centers with strict offtake discipline. He argues these sectors are defensive and supply-constrained today, making current vintages attractive, but warns new entrants will err on school, operator and asset-size selection and that DPI should be the new IRR.

insights.claim: Harrison Street was built as a pure-play 'demographic' alternatives real estate investor (education, healthcare, storage) on the premise that need-based assets avoid the biggest real estate mistakes: market timing and leverage, so entry point matters less.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Need-based, cycle-agnostic sectors let allocators reduce timing risk in real estate allocations.
insights.quote: demographics, it's not trying to time cycles

insights.claim: During the GFC, Harrison Street's need-based assets outperformed their traditional counterparts: medical office beat office, student and senior housing beat multifamily, and storage beat industrial.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Evidence that demographic sectors are defensive in downturns; supports overweighting them in late-cycle portfolios.
insights.quote: Our medical office properties did better than office. Our student senior did better than multi. Our stores are better than industrial.

insights.claim: The original arbitrage was fragmentation: large pension funds and insurers would not do $5-10M one-off deals, so Harrison Street aggregated one-off acquisitions and exited via large portfolio sales; today 80-90% of investments are individual deals while 80-90% of sales are big portfolios.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Aggregation premium (buy small, sell big portfolios) is a repeatable return source in fragmented sectors.
insights.quote: probably 80 80 to 90% of our investments are still individual investments, but 80 to 90% of our sales are through big portfolios

insights.claim: These sectors started with very low institutional ownership (roughly 5-12%), and Merrill argues institutionalization still has 'a long ways to go', implying further cap-rate compression potential.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Ongoing institutionalization is a tailwind for exit pricing in alternative property types.

insights.claim: The market for alternative-sector property sales has grown from roughly 1-2% of the market when Harrison Street started to about 12-15% today, improving liquidity; Harrison Street expects to sell $6-7B of assets this year.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Improved liquidity in alts lowers exit risk and supports DPI for funds in these sectors.
insights.quote: When I started, it was 1 or 2% was probably the market for alternative sales. Now it's maybe 12 to 15 %.

insights.claim: Merrill launched what he describes as the first open-ended core fund that is 100% alternatives (now a 12-14 year track record), arguing core should be defined by capital preservation, low volatility and income, not by the traditional office/industrial/retail/residential sectors.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Core allocators may be under-allocated to alternatives that meet core risk/return criteria.
insights.quote: Core is only office, industrial, retail, residential. We said, well, why not have a core fund

insights.claim: Diversified multi-sector funds are a deliberate risk control: managers forced to deploy all capital into one alternative sector will buy even when that sector's risk/return is poor in a given year.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Prefer diversified alts vehicles over single-sector funds that must deploy regardless of pricing.
insights.quote: If you just have to push all the capital into one asset class, well, if that asset class is not the right risk return in that given year, we don't want to participate.

insights.claim: Lease duration matters for inflation: storage leases reprice monthly and student/senior annually, while medical office has longer leases that are less attractive in an inflationary environment, so a portfolio should not be all medical office.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: In inflationary regimes, favor short-lease alts (storage, student, senior) over long-lease medical office.
insights.quote: storage is monthly, student, senior annual, I can reprice

insights.claim: Student housing diligence revealed the 'Animal House' fear was overstated: purpose-built product renting by the bed with parent guarantees, billing parents for damage and evicting repeat offenders keeps properties in good condition.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Perceived tenant risk in student housing is mitigated by structure (parent guarantees, by-bed leases).
insights.quote: if there's a hole in the wall, we send the bill to the parents and if they do it again, we kick them out

insights.claim: Insurance costs for multifamily exceed those for student housing because the top cause of multifamily insurance claims is kitchen fires, and students rarely use the kitchens.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Non-obvious opex advantage for student housing versus conventional multifamily.
insights.quote: Number one cause of insurance claims in in in student housing or in in multi-family um, is kitchen fires. And the kids don't use the kitchens.

insights.claim: Merrill expects 15-20% of colleges to go out of business, so student housing success depends on picking 'enrollment takers', the right location relative to campus, unit mix and local operator; Harrison Street uses a school-scoring model built over ~1,300 deals and $80B.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Underwrite student housing on school-level enrollment trends, not sector beta; weaker schools are a real credit risk.
insights.quote: there are enrollment takers and then there's probably 15 to 20% of schools will go out of business

insights.claim: Very large student housing assets of 1,200-1,500 beds are too big in Merrill's view; there is a sweet spot in size, bed-bath parity, and proximity to campus.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Be wary of mega student-housing developments that new entrants are building.
insights.quote: A lot of people are doing very large student housing assets that are 1,200 1,500. We think those are very too big.

insights.claim: Senior housing is an operator-intensive, referral-driven business (hospitals, churches) where food service, care continuum and dementia care drive outcomes; multifamily developers entering senior housing underestimate these challenges.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Expect underperformance from generalist entrants in senior housing; operator quality is the key diligence item.
insights.quote: a lot of people that let say are a multi-family developer. Hey, I can build this thing, then I'll now I'll just manage it, but they don't recognize the challenges

insights.claim: Harrison Street's senior housing formula favors independent/assisted/memory care with private pay in the right age- and income-qualified markets; lessons include memory-care-only versus a full continuum of care.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Private-pay, continuum-of-care product in age/income-qualified markets is the preferred senior housing exposure.

insights.claim: Roughly one in three people over 85 have some level of dementia, and senior housing affordability is a growing issue, which shapes choices like private pay versus buy-in CCRCs.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Memory care demand and affordability are key structural drivers for senior housing underwriting.

insights.claim: Self storage is easy to build, so supply is the main risk; Merrill only wants infill, hard-entitlement, high-barrier markets rather than greenfield sites where a competitor can build next door.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Screen storage exposure by entitlement barriers and supply pipeline.
insights.quote: if you go build a storage facility in the middle of a corn field, someone can build one next to you

insights.claim: Self storage has shifted from static rate sheets changed every few months to dynamic pricing that can change every few minutes based on unit occupancy, plus online search ranking that drives customer selection.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Technology/revenue management capability is a differentiator among storage operators and a reason institutional owners outperform mom-and-pops.
insights.quote: dynamic pricing every 5 minutes

insights.claim: Life science real estate has had a challenging run, forcing Harrison Street to re-lease assets, but Merrill remains a long-term believer because 95% of diseases lack a cure.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Life science real estate may be a contrarian long-term opportunity after its downturn.
insights.quote: 95% of all diseases don't have a cure

insights.claim: Harrison Street has done roughly $7-8B in data centers but only with strong credit and offtake: it will not buy land hoping to get power, avoids secondary markets, 'too much AI services' and chasing power.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: A disciplined data-center filter: powered land plus investment-grade offtake; speculative power-chasing is where risk sits.
insights.quote: We don't want to go into secondary markets. We don't want to go into too much AI services. We don't want to chase power.

insights.claim: Within digital infrastructure, Merrill views carrier hotels in city centers as 'very monopolistic' and has invested in a dark fiber business connecting data facilities.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Connectivity assets (carrier hotels, dark fiber) offer monopoly-like economics with less AI capex risk.
insights.quote: carrier hotels, which in our mind are very monopolistic

insights.claim: Merrill sees broad 'essential services' infrastructure as the next frontier: universities and health systems need private capital for housing, district energy, wastewater and data.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Public-private partnerships with universities and hospitals are a growing private infrastructure opportunity set.
insights.quote: the new frontier in a lot of ways is infrastructure

insights.claim: Harrison Street claims to be the largest off-campus owner of student and senior housing and likely the largest owner of on-campus housing, and uses university relationships to expand into district energy and wastewater infrastructure via evergreen 30-year partnerships.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Relationship-driven cross-sell from housing into utility infrastructure creates a moat with institutional offtakers.
insights.quote: we want to be your partners for 30 years

insights.claim: Merrill sees allocations to real estate and infrastructure increasing, driven by inflation worries and a flight to safety in hard assets, while investors are wary of private equity financial engineering and venture capital's very low DPIs.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Watch for flows rotating from PE/VC to real assets and real estate debt.
insights.quote: Venture capital, the DPIs are very very low.

insights.claim: Current vintages are attractive because new supply has been 'absolutely choked off' by tight capital while demand grows (about 2 million people turning 80 every year).
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Supply-constrained alt sectors set up strong rent growth for 2020s vintages; favor deploying now.
insights.quote: supply has been absolutely choked off

insights.claim: Merrill assumes rates stay higher for longer but eventually decline, and expects investors to look back in 5-6 years and be very pleased with today's vintages.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Patient capital deployed in high-rate environment could capture the eventual rate decline.
insights.quote: We're going to look back in 5 6 years and be very excited about it.

insights.claim: Merrill argues 'DPI should be the new IRR': managers should be judged on capital actually returned to investors.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: LPs should prioritize realized distributions over reported IRR when selecting managers.
insights.quote: DPI should be the new IRR

insights.claim: LPs want fewer manager relationships (e.g., from 40 managers to 10), driving consolidation and forcing managers to offer multiple products across geographies, equity, debt and infrastructure to stay relevant.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Expect continued alternative manager consolidation; multi-product platforms gain share.
insights.quote: if they had 40 managers and they want to go to 10

insights.claim: New entrants are crowding into student, senior and storage because office and retail are hard to raise for; Merrill expects missteps from wrong schools, wrong operators, wrong care levels and oversized assets, and says raising billions for self storage is 'almost impossible' to deploy without sacrificing quality.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of large single-sector alt funds; overcapitalized strategies may underperform, while incumbents benefit as sellers.
insights.quote: when you raise billions of dollars to invest in self storage, that's almost impossible

insights.claim: Harrison Street was started around 2004-2005 as a 50/50 partnership with Chris Galvin's family office (former Motorola chairman/CEO), with a first fund of about $200M; the name comes from Motorola's origin on Harrison Street in Chicago.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Context for the platform's origins and anchor capital.

insights.claim: Galvin instilled a Six Sigma 'where are the defects' process: identify likely mistakes in advance (recourse, excess leverage, market timing) and build them into the investment process; Harrison Street keeps a dozen-lesson list per asset class and avoids recourse and cost-overrun risk.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: A pre-mortem/defect framework is a useful manager-diligence lens.
insights.quote: We don't take recourse risk. We don't take cost overruns.

insights.claim: Merrill views innovation in commodity-like real estate as lower risk, not higher, because a first mover has the space to itself; he cites Galvin's advice that when experts say you can't do something, you are onto something.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: First-mover niches in commoditized asset classes can offer better risk-adjusted returns.
insights.quote: when experts tell you you can't do something, you know you're onto something

insights.claim: Merrill evaluates operating partners by asking about their mistakes, desired relationship and succession planning, preferring partners with strong balance sheets that can fund pre-development and take recourse; some partners have done 40-50 deals with Harrison Street over 20 years.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Repeat-partner programmatic JVs create value through rinse-and-repeat efficiency.
insights.quote: tell me the mistakes you've made

insights.claim: About eight or nine years ago Harrison Street sold a stake to Colliers, which lacked an investment management arm, to buy out the Galvin family, gain an evergreen institutional partner, and move equity and carry to the next generation.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Example of GP-stake/succession structuring; Colliers built IM to match Jones Lang (LaSalle) and CBRE.

insights.claim: Harrison Street later combined with Colliers-backed managers Rockwood (real estate debt), Basalt (closed-end infrastructure) and Versus (private wealth) into one platform with about $110B of AUM across North America and Europe, equity, debt and infrastructure, open- and closed-end funds.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Colliers' investment management platform is a scaled alts manager; relevant to Colliers valuation and wealth-channel distribution.
insights.quote: we're 110 billion of AUM

insights.claim: Merrill argues the asset management business has become expensive (investment in people and data, centralized distribution), driving scale consolidation; the platform now serves institutional and retail/RIA/wirehouse channels.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Scale and private-wealth distribution are becoming prerequisites for alt managers.
insights.quote: It's an expensive business now.

insights.claim: In the late 1990s Merrill found Budapest office buildings yielding 13-15% cap rates versus about 5% in Vienna an hour away with the same tenants, construction and credit; the gap was liquidity, which he bet would arrive as countries joined NATO and the EU.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Liquidity premia in opaque markets compress as institutional access improves; a template for frontier real estate.
insights.quote: Budapest, I could invest in an office building and get a 13 14 15 cap rate. Vienna, an hour away, was five.

insights.claim: He avoided Ukraine and Russia (non-NATO) as too much risk with no commensurate upside, focusing on countries where 10-12 year leases repaid capital in five to six years while awaiting EU convergence.
insights.speaker: Christopher Merrill
insights.so_what: Geopolitical anchoring is key to frontier real estate risk/return.
insights.quote: Ukraine, Russia, too much risk
